sec.title: Background
sec.p: Antimicrobial peptide (AMP) prediction has been extensively studied in recent years. However, many existing models do not fully leverage the intrinsic chemical structures of AMPs, such as atomic composition and sidechain group characteristics. Instead, these models often focus on letter composition, positional encodings, and pre-defined chemical-physical descriptors. The incorporation of non-canonical amino acids, which enhance peptide stability and reduce toxicity, is getting more attention in peptide design. Despite this, they are overlooked in predictive studies, as traditional deciphering methods and single-letter representation systems are inadequate for this task. Even though some efforts have been made to expand current alphabets, these approaches remain insufficient, impeding the development of novel AMPs.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A novel deep learning model, termed AmpHGT, was developed based on heterogeneous graphs’ representation of peptides. AmpHGT demonstrates competitive performance against current methods on canonical amino acid benchmarks. Notably, AmpHGT is capable of efficiently classifying antimicrobial peptides with non-canonical amino acids, addressing the limitations of traditional feature extraction methods. In addition, this model is adaptable to handling different conformations, sidechains, and backbones (e.g., α, β, γ), demonstrating its potential to enhance the screening and discovery of AMPs containing non-canonical amino acids.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our study suggests that AmpHGT is reliable for antimicrobial peptide classification task. It may serve as an efficient primary filter for evaluating thousands of mined peptides and provides a good foundation for future studies aimed at producing peptide antibiotics containing non-canonical amino acids.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: The discovery of antibiotics in the twentieth century revolutionized the treatment of bacterial infections. However, the widespread use of antibiotics in healthcare and agriculture has led to the emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a serious threat to global health. In 2019, bacterial AMR and its complications were associated with approximately 4.95 million deaths. Multidrug-resistant bacteria, particularly the ESKAPE pathogens—Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species—are increasingly resistant to existing antibiotics [1].

With the decline of the traditional “Waksman platform” for antibiotic discovery, research has increasingly shifted toward genome mining for natural antimicrobial products, particularly antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) containing non-canonical amino acids (NCAAs). AMPs are of particular interest due to their prolonged resistance development time, potent antimicrobial efficacy, and lower incidence of resistance compared to synthetic antibiotics. Their mechanism of action involves disrupting bacterial cell membranes, altering permeability, and causing cell lysis, making them less susceptible to resistance [2–4].

Recent advancements in computer science have significantly enhanced antibiotic discovery. Models are now capable of accurately predicting the antimicrobial activity or minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of peptides, facilitating high-throughput screening of large peptide datasets obtained through genome mining or chemical space exploration. These computational approaches expedite the identification of promising AMPs, reducing the need for extensive experimental testing and accelerating the discovery process [5, 6].

Various learning methods have been introduced to address AMP prediction problems. The most common approaches are classifiers and generators. Classifiers determine whether the input sequence is an AMP, while generators, typically based on autoregressive models trained on AMP sequences, generate potential new AMPs. For instance, AmPEP by Bhadra et al. implemented a random forest classifier trained on AMP sequences encoded by amino acid distribution patterns to classify peptides [7]. AMPScanner by Veltri et al. employs a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network to predict antimicrobial probability [8]. Huang et al. developed a machine-learning pipeline combining XGBoost and LSTM to explore possible amino acid combinations of lengths 6–9, validating the top MIC peptides [9]. Ma et al. utilized a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model as part of a pipeline integrated with Multi-Omics approach to mine potential AMPs in human gut microbiomes [10]. Wang et al. leveraged 3D structural and sequence information to predict and generate peptides with potent antimicrobial activity [11]. Szymczak et al. developed HydrAMP, a conditional variational autoencoder, to generate potent AMPs [12].

Despite these advances, most studies continue to rely on a standardized workflow for encoding peptides using predefined feature descriptors, such as compositions, autocorrelation methods (e.g., Moran and Geary), frequency-domain features, and physicochemical properties [7, 13–15]. Alternatively, some studies extract features through position encoding or leverage Transformer and BERT models to learn sequence information [16–18]. These approaches primarily focus on contextual classification by modeling character positions, composition, and phase relationships [19]. More recently, Yan et al. employed Graph Attention Networks (GAT) and incorporated predicted 3D structures to improve AMP activity prediction [20]. Pretrained protein language models (PLMs) and conformer prediction models, such as ProtTrans [21], the Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM) suite [22], and AlphaFold [23], have transformed protein deep learning technologies. Leveraging AlphaFold2’s predicted distance thresholds, Zhao et al. represented protein structures as graph data by encoding node features with a pretrained Bi-LSTM protein language model [24]. Similarly, Cordoves-Delgado et al. developed the esm-AxP-GDL framework, which integrates advanced protein structure prediction, evolutionary language models, and graph neural networks to achieve state-of-the-art performance in AMP prediction using learned features rather than physicochemical descriptors [25].

However, most studies often overlook structural variations in amino acids and terminal modifications. NCAAs are either represented by the placeholder “X” in sequence or excluded from analyses entirely. As a result, these methods are incapable of processing the extensive NCAA space [26], which represents a vast area for exploration. Peptides containing NCAAs exhibit enhanced stability and potent antimicrobial activities [27]; most are non-ribosomal peptides (NRPs) such as Brevicidine and Laterocidine [28], Teixobactin [29], Clovibactin [30], Cilagicin [31], Corbomycin [32], and the well-known Vancomycin [33]. The growing interest in incorporating NCAAs into antimicrobial peptides to improve their properties is gaining more attention. Their distinct sidechains and/or conformations can confer novel biochemical properties to newly designed or discovered peptides [34, 35].

This gap underscores the need for modeling approaches that fulfill two key criteria:
Independence from predefined feature extractors that are incompatible with NCAA chemistry.
Scalability and effectiveness comparable to current state-of-the-art methods.

Recent studies have successfully leveraged chemical structure-based approaches to identify small-molecule antibiotics, such as Halicin [36] and Abaucin [37], as well as to develop predictive models [38, 39]. Notably, H. Chang et al. proposed a method employing Gaussian process regression (GPR) to predict peptides represented by the Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES). Their approach calculated over 200 physicochemical descriptors for each peptide, successfully incorporated a limited NCAA dataset, and designed analogs with potent antifungal activity.

Building on recent advancements, we propose a manual feature engineering-free, heterogeneous graph-based model, termed AmpHGT, to address the challenges of representing NCAAs in peptide classification. Unlike conventional PLM-based approaches [25, 40, 41], AmpHGT represents peptides as chemical compound graphs, explicitly modeling amino acid backbones, NCAA sidechains, and pretrained embeddings. This structure allows for a richer representation than single-letter encoding while being more straightforward for constructing heterogeneous graphs compared to the Hierarchical Editing Language for Macromolecules (HELM). Overall, AmpHGT enhances antimicrobial peptide classification by integrating multi-view structural information, enabling the processing of over 600 NCAAs in addition to the 20 canonical amino acids (CAAs).

sec.title: Workflow of AmpHGT
sec.p:
In this study, we employed a multi-view heterogeneous graph to represent peptide structures, facilitating informative peptide structure embedding. Residue-level embeddings were extracted using the pretrained protein language model ESM2 (esm2_t33_650M_UR50D) as recommended in previous study [42]. Peptides were represented at four levels: atom, fragment, residue, and junction (see “Representing peptides as heterogeneous molecular graphs”). This multi-view approach enables the model to capture peptide structures with fine granularity, allowing it to differentiate amino acids based on their similarities, differences, and contributions to peptide properties, such as antimicrobial activity. Finally, we trained the model on labeled data to perform a binary classification task (Fig. 1).Fig. 1
Workflow of this study. Peptides in curated datasets are first converted from sequences to linear structures with terminal modifications, including N-terminal acetylation and C-terminal amidation when available. These batch data are then input into the model for training, resulting in a final model capable of classifying peptides containing NCAAs. 2D SMILES and their corresponding sequence information are fed into the model. Sequence information (residues) is processed by ESM2 to extract the < cls > classification token and residue token embeddings. These embeddings are assigned to the"residue"view in a heterogeneous graph based on residue positional order. The skeletal formula-based molecular graph is divided into two views: an"atom"view and a"fragment"view. The fragment view undergoes fragmentation using our proposed Fragmentize SideChain Even Sub-Sidechain (FraSCESS) method to generate biologically meaningful sub-fragments. Each view is processed through a modified PharmHGT Encoder for multi-layer message passing. The updated graph representations are then aggregated using a GRU-based graph readout to generate graph-level embeddings. The graph-level embeddings are fused with the ESM2-derived < cls > token via bilinear fusion, producing a comprehensive representation of the peptide sequence. This representation is fed into a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to generate final classification logits

sec.title: Performance benchmark on CAA test dataset
sec.p:
To evaluate the performance of AmpHGT in classifying peptides containing CAAs, we compared it against several state-of-the-art (SOTA) AMP recognition methods. To ensure a fair comparison, all benchmarking data were restricted to peptides containing only CAAs. The XUAMP dataset served as the independent test set for all models (see “Datasets”). Previous studies have applied various SOTA AMP recognition methods to classify the dataset and compute performance metrics. These models included amPEPpy [43], ampir [44], AMPScanner vr 2 [8], and AmPEP [7], TP-LMMSG [40], sAMPpred-GAT [20], and additional models. Initially, we assessed both models using a zero-shot approach, where AmpHGT demonstrated slightly better performance than ESM2, achieving a 0.6% increase in MCC and a 0.8% improvement in accuracy.

Subsequently, to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in incremental few-shot learning, we created a joint dataset by combining the CAA dataset with the NCAA overlap dataset and trained the model from scratch. When evaluated on the NCAA independent test dataset, the results showed that while both models performed similarly in the zero-shot setting, ESM2’s predictive performance declined after joint training, whereas AmpHGT’s performance improved by 3.82%, as anticipated. sec.title: Investigation to constructed NCAA dataset
sec.p: As noted in the section “Performance benchmark on NCAA test dataset,” ESM2 and AmpHGT exhibited comparable performance on zero-shot tasks. This outcome was expected, as both models generated predictions based solely on learned canonical features, without prior exposure to NCAA data. The confusion matrices indicate that both models maintained high predictive accuracy for non-antimicrobial peptide sequences, consistent with their strong sensitivity values (Fig. 2). However, both models exhibited a higher false-negative rate when predicting antimicrobial peptide sequences.

Moreover, the strong zero-shot performance on non-antimicrobial peptides from UniProt suggests that their non-antimicrobial nature primarily stems from their canonical amino acid composition. This observation aligns with prior findings: most studies have investigated whether NCAA incorporation enhances the antimicrobial activity or stability of a sequence rather than conferring antimicrobial properties on otherwise inactive sequences [34, 35]. Nevertheless, further research is needed to elucidate how NCAA incorporation influences antimicrobial peptide secondary structures, particularly since this study primarily focused on predictions for linear peptide sequences. It is also important to consider that, in practical applications, complex structural modifications—such as cyclopeptides, depsipeptides, and thiopeptides—play a crucial role in modulating antimicrobial peptide activity [31, 45, 46]. Despite these complexities, most studies, including ours, continue to model linear peptide sequences.

The training sequence lengths in the overlap dataset differed significantly between the positive (22.13 ± 14.21) and negative (35.50 ± 18.93) subsets. According to Sidorczuk et al., ensuring similar sequence lengths during training is essential to prevent the model from using length as a distinguishing feature [47]. However, due to the limited availability of NCAA data, imposing a balanced length cutoff for negative sequences (Fig. 3A) would exclude all sequences longer than 47 residues (Fig. 3B) from analysis. To preserve as many training samples as possible and to avoid length cutoff to any partition, we opted not to adjust sequence lengths in the overlap dataset.Fig. 3
Mean length difference and best cutoff threshold length distribution. A Analysis of different length cutoffs and mean length differences. B Positive and negative sequence length distribution at best threshold

An analysis of NCAA occurrence ratios revealed that 468 NCAA types unique to positive sequences appeared 7767 times in test samples, whereas 57 NCAA types unique to negative sequences occurred 2025 times (Fig. 4A). This disparity in sequence length and NCAA frequency resulted in a subset of positive sequences being predominantly represented as < mask > tokens from ESM2’s perspective—a limitation also observed in AmpHGT in the absence of additional fine-tuning.Fig. 4
Analysis to NCAAs in the non-canonical dataset. A Unique NCAA types that are exclusive to the positive or negative training set and their total frequencies in the respective dataset. B The top 10 NCAAs occurrence in the positive and negative sequences. C Heatmap for frequencies of NCAAs in the overlapped NCAA sequences in training set, Cysteine methyl ester (Cys-OMe), D-serine (D-Ser(Ser)), and D-Threonine (D-Thr) are included in the overlapped NCAAs, but sequences with them are also with unique NCAA types, they are therefore no counts in the overlap dataset

On the joint dataset, AmpHGT performed as expected, demonstrating improvements across multiple metrics (Table 2), including up to a 10% increase in specificity. In contrast, ESM2’s performance declined relative to its zero-shot results. The joint dataset contained a high proportion of NCAA sequences that were largely represented as < mask > tokens, limiting ESM2’s ability to extract meaningful features and leading to increased confusion and reduced performance.

Among positive samples, diamino butyrate (Dab), ornithine (Orn), and norleucine (Nle) collectively accounted for approximately 27.1% of all NCAA residues. This aligns with common antimicrobial peptide engineering strategies, as both Dab and Orn are positively charged under most pH conditions and resistant to degradation, making them prevalent in antimicrobial peptide sequences [48]. In contrast, in negative samples, 4-aspartylphosphate (4-Appp) alone comprised 58.6% of all NCAA residues (Fig. 4B).

Finally, we evaluated AmpHGT’s predictive performance on the top 10 NCAAs in the positive NCAA-independent test set. Detailed results and the corresponding amino acid distribution are provided in Additional file 1: Figure S1, Table 1.

sec.title: Ablation analysis
sec.p:
In this section, we conduct an ablation study to evaluate the impact of different readout methods and the incorporation of the ESM2 pretrained model on the XUAMP test dataset. Specifically, we assessed the effects of average, sum, and max pooling. For cases without pooling, we explored various readout strategies, including attention-based and GRU-based graph readouts. Additionally, we evaluated the improvements introduced by ESM2 (denoted as noESM2) and residue-level subgraphs (denoted as apj, if without residue-level view). The results indicate that, with ESM2 incorporated into the pipeline, both max pooling and GRU-based readout produced similar performance. Notably, the"AmpHGT_GRU"configuration achieved the highest accuracy (0.7365 ± 0.0089), while max pooling yielded the highest MCC, though the improvement was only 0.3%. As a result, we selected AmpHGT_GRU as the primary model for this study. These findings align with conclusions drawn by most state-of-the-art models, which suggest that incorporating pre-trained protein language models can significantly enhance the performance of lightweight models in antimicrobial peptide classification. Although PharmHGT with lightweight Sequence Encoder (AmpHGT_noESM2) can distinguish some positive and negative samples, its performance is reduced by approximately 5% in terms of accuracy compared to the combined ESM2 model, every single experiment’s metrics can be found in Additional file 1: Table 2.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, AmpHGT enhances message passing across multiple peptide views and demonstrates superior performance, particularly in classifying peptides containing non-canonical amino acids (NCAAs), compared to ESM2. The integration of sequence embeddings with graph-based relational learning (section “Investigation to constructed NCAA dataset”) effectively addresses critical limitations of purely sequence-driven approaches. Notably, our joint training paradigm achieves higher predictive accuracy than ESM2 alone for NCAA-rich antimicrobial peptides.

However, four key limitations of current methodologies warrant attention. First, our multi-view representation approach does not incorporate secondary structural features such as helices and folds. Second, the model primarily focuses on linear peptide structures, despite the prevalence of cyclic architectures in natural antimicrobial peptides, including Brevicidine [28], Nisin [49], and Vancomycin [33]. Third, dataset constraints present significant challenges, particularly the limited overlap of NCAAs between positive and negative samples and discrepancies between synthetic peptide representations and physiological structures, which may contribute to underfitting [50]. Fourth, this study entirely omits the predefined physicochemical properties of amino acids, which may impact predictive performance.

Notwithstanding these limitations, a comprehensive evaluation confirms that AmpHGT’s combination of sequence embedding and HGT performs comparably to sequence embedding and 3D conformer-based approaches. Notably, AmpHGT offers a lightweight alternative by eliminating the need for 3D structure generation. Furthermore, if molecular structures—including ring formations and amino-amino interactions such as head-to-tail cyclization and disulfide bridges—are accurately annotated with correct SMILES representations, AmpHGT could theoretically be extended to accommodate these features.

Most pretrained protein language models (e.g., ESM2, ProtTrans) are restricted to the 20 canonical amino acids due to their training on UniRef datasets. Although the Protein Data Bank contains proteins with over 1000 distinct NCAAs, current 3D conformer prediction models offer limited support for post-translational modifications and NCAAs. While Rosetta is flexible enough to expand its predictions to NCAAs, configuring conformational relationships for each amino acid remains highly complex and computationally demanding. Recent efforts to address these challenges include the introduction of CyclicBoltz1 by Xie et al. within the AlphaFold3 framework, enabling efficient and accurate prediction of cyclic peptide structures and complexes containing non-canonical amino acids (NCAAs) [51]. While the integration of 3D structural features—such as atomic coordinates and intra-subgraph residue distances—has shown promise in canonical peptide prediction, their incorporation into heterogeneous graph transformer (HGT)-based representations for NCAAs remains underexplored.

As demonstrated by Chang et al. in their study on antifungal peptide analogs [39], integrating handcrafted features with learned embeddings can enhance predictive performance on NCAA datasets. Supporting this direction, Milchevskiy et al. extended the AAindex to include NCAAs [52], and Oeller et al. developed CamSol-PTM to accurately predict physicochemical properties of peptides containing NCAAs [53]. These advancements provide a foundation for future research to evaluate the synergistic benefits of combining handcrafted features with the HGT framework.

Finally, in light of recent progress in generative models for antimicrobial peptide design [12, 54] and heterogeneous graph-based molecular generation [55], future work should move beyond the current classification capabilities of AmpHGT. Specifically, there is significant potential in exploring the de novo generation of heterogeneous graph representations for AMPs with complex secondary structures, followed by experimental validation of their antimicrobial activity.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, we present AmpHGT, a deep learning model based on a modified heterogeneous graph transformer, specifically designed for AMP classification. Rigorous assessment shows that this model is capable of classifying peptides containing both canonical and non-canonical amino acids.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this section, we provide an overview of our strategy. We first introduce the molecule fragmentation method, termed"Fragmentize SideChain Even Sub-Sidechain"(FraSCESS). We then describe the architecture of the model used, detail the training process, and explain the sourcing and processing of the datasets.

sec.title: Representing peptides as heterogeneous molecular graphs
sec.p: Based on prior studies [56–58], we incorporate fragments and atom-level representations into molecular graphs, considering the nature of peptides, we also introduced residue-level representation in to the molecular graphs to enhance the representation of molecular and peptide properties. sec.title: Mapping method
sec.p: Subsequently, we created a vocabulary for fragments by cleaving all FraSCESS bonds in generated pseudo peptides (Gly – NCAAs – Gly, Gly – NCAAs, and NCAAs—Gly) to explore possible linear combinations of peptides, resulting in the size of 358 fragments to cover most of the possible situation in our dataset. Then, a mapping function m is created for transforming each atom, fragment, and residue into a fixed-length vector, in other words, all nodes and edges in subgraphs are represented by feature matrices here. For atom-level view, features are assembled by atom number, degree, formal charge, chiral tag, number of Hs, and Hybridization. For fragment-level view, features are assembled by fingerprint from Molecular ACCess System and RDkit ChemicalFeatures factory. For residue-level view, features are split from ESM2 embeddings to token level and append by positions.

sec.title: Encoder architecture
sec.p: We used a modified PharmHGT [57] by Pepland [56] for peptides as our graph encoder, PharmHGT, which is a pharmacophoric-constrained heterogeneous graph transformer model for molecular property prediction (Fig. 6A). sec.title: CAA dataset collection
sec.p: In this study, datasets containing only canonical amino acids were the XUAMP dataset obtained from TP_LMMSG, the XUAMP dataset is integrated from multiple datasets including APD3, DRAMP, LAMP, CAMP, dbAMP, YADAMP, and UniProt, resulting in 5536 AMPs/nonAMPs in the training set, and 1536 AMPs/nonAMPs in the independent test set. The XUAMP test set is an independent test set initially proposed by Xu et al. through rigorous filtering, served as the primary evaluation benchmark [62]. Additionally, we also collected AMPDiscover dataset proposed by Pinacho-Castellanos et al., the AMPDiscover set is comprised of 19,548 training, 5125 validation, and 15,685 test peptide sequences. The positive sequences of the AMPDiscover were obtained from starPepDB database. The negative sequences are obtained following common procedures. We have also obtained the external test created by G Cordoves-Delgado et al. for model comparison [25, 63]. Detailed information on the CAA datasets can be found in the Additional file 1: Figure S2-S3, Table 3.

sec.title: NCAA dataset collection
sec.p: The NCAA dataset was sourced from DBAASP [64] and UniProt [65], to the best of our knowledge, the DBAASP is the only antimicrobial peptide database that records detailed NCAA information in peptides, including their position and category. Positive non-canonical amino acid-containing peptides (NCAA-AMP) were sourced from DBAASP with search criteria: “Complexity: Monomer,” “Target Group (Multi select): Gram +, Gram −.” For UniProt peptides, only reviewed entries containing at least one of the keywords “Antimicrobial,” “Antibiotic,” or “Amphibian defense peptide” and excluding sequences without residue modifications were included.

Negative non-canonical amino acid-containing peptides (NCAA-non-AMP) were sourced using the same search criteria as the NCAA-AMP but excluded entries containing keywords related to “Antimicrobial,” “Antibiotic,” “Amphibian defense peptide,” “Antiviral protein,” and related terms.

All sequences were cleaned by removing ambiguous characters and duplicates. Sequences outside the length range of 2 to 60 amino acids were excluded (some peptides in DBAASP have only 1 amino acid but a bulk terminal modification which was not incorporated in this study, e.g., LP1 ~ 6 [66]). The initial NCAA datasets comprised NCAA-AMP: 3780 and NCAA-non-AMP: 3652 sequences. All data were sourced as of July 15, 2024.

sec.title: NCAA dataset processing
sec.p: Following initial data collection, CD-HIT was not implemented here control sequence similarity because of the expanded residue alphabet this dataset has, we refined the NCAA-containing sequences through two-stage filtering. First, 3036 AMPs and 2792 non-AMPs with true NCAA residues were retained after excluding sequences with solely terminal modifications (e.g., C-terminal amidation). Comparative analysis revealed significant NCAA diversity differences: AMPs contained 486 unique NCAAs versus 84 in non-AMPs.

To prevent the model from relying on unique amino acids present in different sequence sets to distinguish between antimicrobial and non-antimicrobial peptides, we selected the intersection of the two sequence sets as the training sequences, creating an"overlap"training set—NCAA overlap dataset. Initial intersection contained 29 NCAA types, reduced to 26 after removing D-Thr, D-Ser, and Cys-OMe whose co-occurring residues were group-specific. This overlap set included 340 AMPs and 893 non-AMPs, with the latter downsampled to 340 to balance class distribution, the NCAA overlap dataset was then split by 8:2 to create training and validating set.

Subsequent data partitioning allocated sequences with unique NCAAs per group into the NCAA-independent test set (AMPs = 2696; non-AMPs = 2452), while combining the overlap set with standard CAA training data formed the joint training dataset for zero-shot evaluation (Fig. 7A).Fig. 7
Processing of NCAA data. A Collecting and processing the NCAA containing sequences, the overlapped NCAAs containing sequences were used for training. Other sequences were used as independent test set. B Length distribution of the NCAA datasets

sec.title: Length distribution of the NCAA overlap dataset
sec.p: For antimicrobial peptide sequences, the length distribution was as follows: mean: 13.06, median: 11.00, standard deviation: 7.54. For non-antimicrobial peptide sequences, the length distribution was as follows: mean: 47.39, median: 54.00, standard deviation: 14.79 (Fig. 7B, Additiona file 1: Table 3). Although there is a significant difference in length between these sequences, posing a risk that the model might distinguish positive and negative sequences based on length, we did not impose any restrictions on length distribution, considering the scarcity of data and the potential for joint training to mitigate this issue, also discussed in “Investigation to constructed NCAA dataset.”
All sequences were converted into peptide SMILES representations for training. Detailed dataset distribution and NCAA types can be found in Additional file 1: Tables 3–4 and Additional file 2.

sec.title: Implementation details
sec.p: All training and inference were conducted on Linux with NVIDIA Tesla P40 24 GB, 32 GB RAM, PyTorch version 2.3.1, CUDA version 11.8.
